Core idea

A probability distribution assigns mass or density to possible outcomes. Discrete models sum point probabilities; continuous probabilities are areas under a density curve.

How to work it

Match mechanism to model: fixed trials for binomial, event counts for Poisson, waiting times for exponential, and bell-shaped measurements for normal.

Watch for

For a continuous distribution, probability at one exact point is zero even when density there is positive.

Three worked examples

Use the lab controls to test these relationships.

2

P(X=0)=e^(−3)≈0.050.
3
Heights

P(160<X<180)≈0.683 by the ±1σ rule.

Core idea

Inverse trig functions return principal angles after restricting the original function to a one-to-one branch. Arcsin returns [-π/2,π/2], arccos [0,π], and arctan (-π/2,π/2).

How to work it

Check the input domain, find the reference angle, then select the principal value in the inverse function's range.

Watch for

arcsin(sinθ) need not equal θ outside the principal range.

Principal value is 120°.

title: Heat & Wave Equation Modes
text:
Core idea

A partial differential equation relates derivatives in several independent variables. Separated sine modes satisfy homogeneous Dirichlet boundaries on a finite interval.

How to work it

For heat, multiply sin(nπx/L) by exp(−κ(nπ/L)²t). For a wave with zero initial velocity, multiply it by cos(cnπt/L).

Watch for

A separated mode is one special solution. General initial data require a convergent series of modes; boundary and initial conditions determine coefficients.

Three worked examples

Use the lab controls to test these relationships.

1
Heat mode

L=π, n=1, κ=1, amplitude=1.

u=e^(−t)sin x.
2
Wave mode

L=π, n=2, c=1.

u=cos(2t)sin(2x), with zero initial velocity.
3
Boundary check

Evaluate any sine mode at x=0 and x=L.

Both values are zero for integer n.
Test it in the live lab

title: Boundary-Value Eigenfunctions
text:
me examples
Try these
Core idea

Boundary-value problems prescribe values at different spatial points, rather than all data at one initial point. Nonzero solutions of an eigenvalue problem exist only at allowed spectral values.

How to work it

For −u″=λu with u(0)=u(L)=0, use sine solutions: λₙ=(nπ/L)² and uₙ=A sin(nπx/L), n≥1.

Watch for

A zero function satisfies the homogeneous equation for every λ; an eigenfunction must be nonzero. Other boundary conditions give different spectra.

Three worked examples

Use the lab controls to test these relationships.

1
First mode

L=π, n=1.

λ=1 and u=sin x.
2
Second mode

L=π, n=2.

λ=4 and u=sin(2x), with one interior zero.
3
Interval scale

Double L with fixed n.

λ_new=λ_old/4; the eigenvalue becomes one quarter as large.
Test it in the live lab

Change the domain length.

Only discrete eigenvalues admit nonzero modes.
